key_terms.meaning: A signal band-limited to f<sub>max</sub> is fully determined by its samples if f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub>.
The minimum sampling rate 2f<sub>max</sub> of a signal band-limited to f<sub>max</sub>.
X<sub>s</sub>(f) = (1/T<sub>s</sub>) Σ X(f − kf<sub>s</sub>): copies of X(f) every f<sub>s</sub>.
The gap from f<sub>max</sub> to f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>max</sub> between the baseband and the first copy; width f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>max</sub>.
x(t) = Σ x(nT<sub>s</sub>) sinc((t − nT<sub>s</sub>)/T<sub>s</sub>), with sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu).
Overlap of spectral copies when f<sub>s</sub> < 2f<sub>max</sub>; a component at f is seen at the nearest |f − kf<sub>s</sub>|.
Analog low-pass filter before the sampler; Butterworth order N ≥ log₁₀(10<sup>A/10</sup> − 1)/(2 log₁₀(f<sub>stop</sub>/f<sub>c</sub>)).
2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1) for an integer m with 1 ≤ m ≤ ⌊f<sub>H</sub>/B⌋, B = f<sub>H</sub> − f<sub>L</sub>.
Flat-top sampling multiplies the spectrum by τ sinc(fτ)e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>; gain 2/π ≈ 0.637 at f<sub>s</sub>/2 for τ = T<sub>s</sub>.
Δ = (x<sub>max</sub> − x<sub>min</sub>)/L with L = 2ⁿ levels for n bits.
e<sub>q</sub> = Q(x) − x, uniform on ±Δ/2, power Δ²/12.
y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k]; length N₁ + N₂ − 1 for finite sequences.
Σ|h[n]| finite; causal when h[n] = 0 for n < 0.
Σ a<sub>k</sub> y[n − k] = Σ b<sub>m</sub> x[n − m], a<sub>0</sub> = 1; order N = largest output delay.
λ<sup>N</sup> + a<sub>1</sub>λ<sup>N−1</sup> + … + a<sub>N</sub> = 0; its roots are the natural modes (poles).
A causal LCCDE system is stable if and only if every |λ<sub>i</sub>| < 1.

takeaways: Sampling at f<sub>s</sub> copies the spectrum every f<sub>s</sub>; if f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub> the copies stay apart and an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 and gain T<sub>s</sub> rebuilds x(t).
Below the Nyquist rate a component at f is seen at the nearest |f − kf<sub>s</sub>|, and no processing of the samples can undo it.
The anti-aliasing filter is analog and sits before the sampler; sampling faster widens the guard band and lowers the filter order it needs.
A band from f<sub>L</sub> to f<sub>H</sub> can be sampled at 2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1), often far below 2f<sub>H</sub>.
Flat-top (sample-and-hold) sampling droops by sinc(fτ), the aperture effect; short pulses or an inverse-sinc equalizer correct it.
An n-bit uniform quantizer has step Δ = range/2ⁿ, noise power Δ²/12 and SQNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine.
A discrete-time LTI system is described completely by h[n]; its output is the convolution sum, and it is stable when Σ|h[n]| is finite.
A difference equation is solved by iteration or as natural plus forced response; it is stable when every characteristic root is inside the unit circle.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine the sampling theorem with aliasing and a numerical alias or band-pass question, and most syllabi that list practical sampling ask for the aperture effect with its sinc factor. On the discrete-time side, expect one convolution-sum evaluation and one difference equation solved in closed form with a stability verdict.

bank.q: State the sampling theorem for a band-limited signal and derive the ideal reconstruction formula using sinc interpolation.
outline: Define a band-limited signal and f<sub>max</sub>
Model sampling by an impulse train and show the spectrum repeats every f<sub>s</sub>
State the condition f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub>
Show that an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 and gain T<sub>s</sub> recovers X(f)
Derive x(t) = Σ x(nT<sub>s</sub>) sinc((t − nT<sub>s</sub>)/T<sub>s</sub>)
answer: Band-limited signal. A signal x(t) is band-limited to fmax if its Fourier transform X(f) = 0 for |f| > fmax. Samples are taken at t = nTs for every integer n, with sampling interval Ts and sampling rate fs = 1/Ts.

Statement. A signal band-limited to fmax is uniquely determined by its samples x(nTs) if fs > 2fmax. The minimum rate 2fmax is the Nyquist rate and the largest spacing 1/(2fmax) is the Nyquist interval.

Impulse-train model. Write the sampled signal as xs(t) = x(t)p(t), with p(t) = Σ δ(t − nTs). Because x(t)δ(t − nTs) = x(nTs)δ(t − nTs), this is xs(t) = Σ x(nTs)δ(t − nTs): each impulse carries one sample as its area.

Spectrum of the impulse train. p(t) is periodic with period Ts. Its exponential Fourier series has every coefficient equal to 1/Ts, so p(t) = (1/Ts) Σ ej2πkfst, and its transform is P(f) = (1/Ts) Σ δ(f − kfs).
Spectrum of the samples. Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency: Xs(f) = X(f) * P(f) = (1/Ts) Σ X(f − kfs). The spectrum is X(f), scaled by 1/Ts, repeated at every multiple of fs.

No overlap. The k = 0 copy occupies −fmax to fmax; the k = 1 copy starts at fs − fmax. They do not overlap when fs − fmax > fmax, that is fs > 2fmax. The strict sign matters: at fs = 2fmax a cosine at fmax can be sampled at its zero crossings and give all-zero samples.

Recovery in frequency. Let H(f) = Ts for |f| < fs/2 and 0 elsewhere. With no overlap, only the k = 0 copy lies inside the passband, so Xs(f)H(f) = (1/Ts)X(f)·Ts = X(f). The filter output is exactly x(t).
Impulse response of the filter. h(t) = ∫ H(f)ej2πft df over −fs/2 to fs/2 = Ts·sin(πfst)/(πt) = sinc(t/Ts), using sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu).

Interpolation formula. The output is xs(t) * h(t) = Σ x(nTs) h(t − nTs), so x(t) = Σ x(nTs) sinc((t − nTs)/Ts). Each pulse is 1 at its own instant and 0 at every other instant nTs, so the formula returns the samples exactly and fills in the curve between them.

answer.text: Numerical check. For x(t) = 3 cos(2π·200t) + 2 cos(2π·450t) sampled at fs = 1000 Hz (fmax = 450 Hz, Nyquist rate 900 Hz), the spectral lines and the filter are:

answer: Closing check. The guard band is 550 − 450 = 100 Hz = fs − 2fmax, so the filter separates the copies. Summing the sinc series at t = 0.5 ms (between two samples) with many terms gives 2.740 V, and the formula 3 cos(0.2π) + 2 cos(0.45π) gives 2.427 + 0.313 = 2.740 V.

bank.q: Explain aliasing using the spectrum of a sampled signal. Define Nyquist rate and Nyquist frequency with an example.
outline: Draw the baseband spectrum and its copies every f<sub>s</sub>
Show the overlap when f<sub>s</sub> < 2f<sub>max</sub>
Define the Nyquist rate 2f<sub>max</sub> and the Nyquist frequency f<sub>s</sub>/2
Give one numerical alias with the folding rule
State that aliasing cannot be undone after sampling and needs an anti-aliasing filter
answer: Spectrum of the samples. Sampling at fs gives Xs(f) = fs Σ X(f − kfs): the spectrum X(f) of width −fmax to fmax is copied at 0, ±fs, ±2fs, …. Sketch the baseband triangle and the same triangle centred at fs.

Overlap. The first copy starts at fs − fmax. If fs > 2fmax this is above fmax and a guard band of width fs − 2fmax separates the copies. If fs < 2fmax, the copy reaches below fmax into the baseband and the two add. That overlap is aliasing: a frequency above fs/2 appears in the samples as a lower one.
Nyquist rate. The minimum sampling rate for a signal band-limited to fmax, 2fmax. It belongs to the signal.
Nyquist frequency. Half the sampling rate, fs/2. It belongs to the sampler: components below it are kept; components above it fold.

Folding rule. A component at f is seen at the value of |f − kfs| nearest to zero over integers k. In the time domain, cos(2πf nTs) = cos(2π(f − kfs)nTs) for every integer n, so the two frequencies give the same samples.

answer.text: Example. Take fs = 1000 Hz, so the Nyquist frequency is 500 Hz.

answer: Reading the table. The 700 Hz and 1300 Hz tones give exactly the samples of a 300 Hz tone. A signal containing 300 Hz and 700 Hz would need fs > 2 × 700 = 1400 Hz (its Nyquist rate) to be sampled correctly.

Irreversible. After sampling, the alias and a real 300 Hz tone are the same numbers, so no digital filter can separate them. The only cure is an analog anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the sampler, which removes components that would fold into the wanted band.

svg.aria: A triangular baseband spectrum up to 700 hertz and its copy centred at 1000 hertz overlapping between 300 and 700 hertz, with the Nyquist frequency of 500 hertz marked and the dashed sum flattened in the overlap.

answer.text: Sketch. The figure shows a triangular spectrum of half-width fmax = 700 Hz sampled at fs = 1000 Hz: the copy centred at 1000 Hz reaches down to 300 Hz, so the band from 300 Hz to 700 Hz is covered twice and the sum (dashed) is no longer the original triangle.

answer: Where the alias lands. A line at f inside the overlap, say 700 Hz, has an image at fs − f = 300 Hz from the copy at fs. The baseband filter (cutoff fs/2 = 500 Hz) passes that image, so the output contains a 300 Hz line that was never in x(t), and loses the true 700 Hz line.

Effect on amplitude. A single aliased cosine keeps its amplitude. When a real component and an aliased one land on the same frequency they add with their phases, so the measured amplitude there can grow or shrink: the original spectrum cannot be read back from the sum.
Closing check. With fs = 1000 Hz: cos(2π·700·n/1000) at n = 1 is cos(1.4π) = −0.309 and cos(2π·300·n/1000) at n = 1 is cos(0.6π) = −0.309; equal, as the folding rule says.

bank.q: Define uniform quantization. Derive the step size and show that quantization noise variance is Δ²/12 for a uniform error model.
outline: Define n-bit uniform quantization and L = 2ⁿ levels
Write Δ = (x<sub>max</sub> − x<sub>min</sub>)/2ⁿ
Model the error e<sub>q</sub> = Q(x) − x as uniform on −Δ/2 to Δ/2
Compute its mean (0) and variance (Δ²/12)
State the assumptions of the model and derive SQNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB
answer: Definition. Quantization maps each sample to the nearest of a finite set of output levels. In an n-bit uniform quantizer the L = 2ⁿ levels are equally spaced, Δ apart.

Step size. If the L steps tile the range xmin to xmax (mid-rise), L steps of width Δ cover xmax − xmin, so Δ = (xmax − xmin)/L = (xmax − xmin)/2ⁿ. The levels sit at xmin + (k + ½)Δ for k = 0, …, L − 1.
Error bound. Rounding to the nearest level gives eq = Q(x) − x with −Δ/2 ≤ eq ≤ Δ/2 while x is inside the range.
Noise model. For a busy signal that crosses many levels, eq is treated as a random variable spread uniformly on (−Δ/2, Δ/2), with probability density 1/Δ there, independent of the signal.
Mean. E[eq] = (1/Δ) ∫ e de from −Δ/2 to Δ/2 = (1/Δ)[e²/2] = (1/Δ)(Δ²/8 − Δ²/8) = 0.
Variance. E[eq²] = (1/Δ) ∫ e² de from −Δ/2 to Δ/2 = (1/Δ)[e³/3] = (1/Δ)(Δ³/24 + Δ³/24) = Δ²/12. Since the mean is zero, the noise power is Pq = Δ²/12.
SQNR. A full-scale sine has A = (xmax − xmin)/2 = LΔ/2 and power A²/2 = L²Δ²/8. SQNR = (L²Δ²/8)/(Δ²/12) = 1.5L² = 1.5 × 4ⁿ, so in dB SQNR = 10 log₁₀ 1.5 + 20n log₁₀ 2 = 1.76 + 6.02n dB.

answer.text: Numbers for a 3-bit, 0 V to 8 V quantizer.

answer: Assumptions. No overload (x stays inside the range), many levels crossed between samples, and an error uncorrelated with the signal. A constant or very slow input breaks the model; dither restores it.

Why uniform is reasonable. When the signal changes by many steps between samples, the position of x inside its step is equally likely anywhere, so eq is equally likely anywhere in ±Δ/2. A sine that spans the whole range at a frequency unrelated to fs behaves this way closely.

Why the noise is called white. Under the same conditions successive errors are nearly uncorrelated, so their power Δ²/12 is spread evenly from 0 to fs/2. This is what makes oversampling useful: only the part of the noise inside the signal band matters.
Mid-tread note. A mid-tread quantizer has a level at zero, so a zero input gives zero error; its noise power is the same Δ²/12 for a busy signal because the error is still spread over one step.
Closing check. 6.02 × 3 + 1.76 = 19.82 dB, the same as 10 log₁₀ 96 = 19.82 dB from the table.

bank.q: Define a discrete-time LTI system and derive its convolution-sum output from the impulse response.
outline: Define linearity and time invariance in discrete time
Write x[n] = Σ x[k]δ[n − k]
Use time invariance and superposition
Obtain y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k]
State the properties and check with a short example
answer: Linearity. A discrete-time system T is linear if T{a x1[n] + b x2[n]} = a y1[n] + b y2[n] for all inputs and constants: it obeys additivity and scaling.
Time invariance. If x[n] gives y[n], then x[n − n0] gives y[n − n0] for every integer shift n0.
Impulse response. h[n] = T{δ[n]} with the system at rest.
Step 1: decompose the input. Every sequence is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses: x[n] = Σk=−∞∞ x[k]δ[n − k], because δ[n − k] picks out the value at n = k.
Step 2: time invariance. T{δ[n − k]} = h[n − k].
Step 3: linearity. x[k] is a constant for each k, so T{x[k]δ[n − k]} = x[k]h[n − k], and the response to the sum is the sum of responses.
Result. y[n] = Σk=−∞∞ x[k]h[n − k] = x[n] * h[n], the convolution sum. Putting m = n − k gives the equivalent form Σ h[m]x[n − m].

Properties. Commutative (x * h = h * x), associative (cascaded systems combine as h1 * h2), distributive (parallel systems add as h1 + h2), identity (x * δ = x). Causal if h[n] = 0 for n < 0; BIBO stable if Σ|h[n]| is finite.

answer.text: Short example. x[n] = [2, 1, 3] and h[n] = [1, 2], both from n = 0:

answer: Why both conditions are needed. Without time invariance the response to δ[n − k] would be a different sequence hk[n] for each k, and the output would be Σ x[k]hk[n], which is not a convolution. Without linearity the response to the sum would not be the sum of responses.

Reading the sum. For a fixed n, the term x[k]h[n − k] is the input at time k weighted by how strongly the system still responds n − k samples later. For a causal system h[n − k] = 0 when k > n, so the sum runs only over the present and past inputs, k ≤ n.

Graphical evaluation. Flip h[k] to h[−k], shift it by n to get h[n − k], multiply sample by sample with x[k] and add. For y[1] in the example below, h[1 − k] has the value 2 at k = 0 and 1 at k = 1, so y[1] = 2·2 + 1·1 = 5.
Closing check. Length 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 samples, and the sum 2 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 18 equals (2 + 1 + 3)(1 + 2) = 18.

bank.q: A signal x(t) = 3 cos(2π·1000t) + 2 cos(2π·3500t) is sampled at f<sub>s</sub> = 4 kHz. Find the alias frequencies and explain whether the original signal can be recovered.
outline: The Nyquist frequency is 2 kHz
1000 Hz is below it and stays at 1000 Hz
The reconstructed signal is 3 cos(2π·1000t) + 2 cos(2π·500t), not x(t)
An anti-aliasing filter or f<sub>s</sub> > 7 kHz was needed
answer: Given. Components at 1000 Hz (3 V) and 3500 Hz (2 V); fs = 4000 Hz, so Ts = 0.25 ms and the Nyquist frequency is fs/2 = 2000 Hz.
Nyquist rate. fmax = 3500 Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 7000 Hz. Since 4000 < 7000, the signal is undersampled.
1000 Hz component. 1000 < 2000, so it is not aliased; it is seen at 1000 Hz.
3500 Hz component. 3500 > 2000. The nearest multiple of 4000 Hz is 4000 Hz, so it is seen at |3500 − 4000| = 500 Hz.

answer.text: Sample check. x[n] = 3 cos(πn/2) + 2 cos(7πn/4), compared with the alias signal 3 cos(πn/2) + 2 cos(πn/4):

answer: Reconstruction. The ideal filter (cutoff 2 kHz, gain Ts) passes the lines at 1000 Hz and 500 Hz and gives xr(t) = 3 cos(2π·1000t) + 2 cos(2π·500t). This is not x(t): the 3500 Hz component has been replaced by a false 500 Hz tone.
Can x(t) be recovered? No. The samples are identical to those of xr(t), so nothing done after sampling can tell which signal produced them.

What was needed. Either sample above the Nyquist rate (for example fs = 8 kHz, giving a guard band 8000 − 7000 = 1000 Hz), or, if only the 1000 Hz part is wanted, put an analog anti-aliasing filter before the sampler that removes 3500 Hz; the output is then 3 cos(2π·1000t) alone, with no false tone.

Spectrum picture. On the positive axis the sampled spectrum has lines at 1000 Hz and at 500 Hz (from 4000 − 3500) inside 0 to 2 kHz, and further lines at 3000 Hz (4000 − 1000), 4500 Hz (8000 − 3500), 5000 Hz (4000 + 1000) and 7500 Hz (4000 + 3500).

Amplitude of the alias. A single cosine keeps its amplitude when it folds, so the false 500 Hz tone has amplitude 2 V, the same as the 3500 Hz component it came from; its phase is reversed in sign, which for a cosine with zero phase makes no difference.

Energy check. The power of x(t) is 3²/2 + 2²/2 = 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 W (into 1 Ω), and the power of the reconstructed signal is the same 6.5 W: aliasing moves power to the wrong frequency rather than losing it, which is why it is so hard to spot.
Closing check. At 8 kHz, 3500 Hz is below fs/2 = 4000 Hz and stays at 3500 Hz; at 4 kHz it appears at 500 Hz, which is below 2000 Hz as every alias must be.

bank.q: A signal has frequency components at 500 Hz, 1.8 kHz and 2.6 kHz. Choose a sampling rate and specify an anti-aliasing filter. Explain your choice.
outline: f<sub>max</sub> = 2.6 kHz, so f<sub>s</sub> must exceed 5.2 kHz
Choose a practical rate such as 8 kHz and find the guard band
Set the filter passband to cover 2.6 kHz and the stopband edge at f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>max</sub>
Find the Butterworth order for the attenuation needed
Check that no component and no strong interference folds into the band
answer: Highest frequency. fmax = 2.6 kHz, so the Nyquist rate is 2 × 2.6 = 5.2 kHz and fs must exceed 5.2 kHz.
Choice. Take fs = 8 kHz, a standard rate. The guard band is 8 − 5.2 = 2.8 kHz (from 2.6 kHz to 5.4 kHz), which leaves room for a real filter. The Nyquist frequency is 4 kHz.
Components after sampling. 0.5, 1.8 and 2.6 kHz are all below 4 kHz, so none is aliased.
Why a filter at all. Noise or interference above 4 kHz would fold into the band: for example a 6 kHz pickup appears at |6 − 8| = 2 kHz, between the 1.8 and 2.6 kHz components.

Filter edges. Passband up to 2.6 kHz; choose the 3 dB cutoff fc = 3 kHz so 2.6 kHz is not cut. Components above fs − fmax = 5.4 kHz fold into 0 to 2.6 kHz, so the stopband edge is fstop = 5.4 kHz. Require A = 40 dB there.

answer.text: Check the design (N = 8, fc = 3 kHz). Attenuation = 10 log₁₀(1 + (f/fc)16):

head: f (kHz)
f/f<sub>c</sub>
Attenuation (dB)
Comment
rows: interference that would land at 2 kHz

answer: Trade-off. A lower rate (say 6 kHz) shrinks the guard band to 0.8 kHz and needs a much steeper filter; a higher rate relaxes the filter but costs more samples per second.

Strict versus usual rule. The strict rule would put the stopband edge at fs/2 = 4 kHz. Components between 4 and 5.4 kHz fold to between 2.6 and 4 kHz, above the highest wanted component, so a digital low-pass filter after the sampler can remove them; that is why the usual rule uses 5.4 kHz and needs a lower order.
Order with the strict rule. With fstop = 4 kHz and fc = 3 kHz: N ≥ 4.000/(2 log₁₀ 1.333) = 4.000/(2 × 0.1249) = 16.0, so N = 17: twice the order, for no gain in the wanted band.
Closing check. fs = 8 kHz > 5.2 kHz; the filter passes 2.6 kHz with 0.42 dB loss and cuts the folding region by at least 40.8 dB.

bank.q: For h[n] = aⁿu[n] with |a| < 1, compute y[n] = x[n] * h[n] when x[n] = u[n] − u[n − 5].
outline: Write y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k]
Use the support of x[k], k = 0 to 4
Insert h[n − k] = a<sup>n−k</sup>u[n − k]
Split into n < 0, 0 ≤ n ≤ 4 and n ≥ 5 and sum the finite geometric series
Give the piecewise answer and check it with a = 0.5
answer: Input. x[n] = u[n] − u[n − 5] is 1 for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 0 elsewhere: five ones.
Sum. y[n] = Σk=04 x[k]h[n − k] = Σk=04 an−ku[n − k]. The factor u[n − k] keeps only the terms with k ≤ n.
Case n < 0. Every k from 0 to 4 has k > n, so all terms vanish: y[n] = 0.
Case 0 ≤ n ≤ 4. Only k = 0 to n survive: y[n] = Σk=0n an−k. Put m = n − k: y[n] = Σm=0n am = (1 − an+1)/(1 − a).
Case n ≥ 5. All five terms survive: y[n] = Σk=04 an−k = an−4(1 + a + a² + a³ + a⁴) = an−4(1 − a⁵)/(1 − a).
Answer. y[n] = 0 for n < 0; (1 − an+1)/(1 − a) for 0 ≤ n ≤ 4; an−4(1 − a⁵)/(1 − a) for n ≥ 5.

Join at n = 4 and 5. The first form at n = 4 gives (1 − a⁵)/(1 − a); the second at n = 4 would give the same value, so the pieces meet. At n = 5 the output is a times the n = 4 value, as expected once the input has stopped.

answer.text: Check with a = 0.5 (direct sum against the formula):

answer: Large n. For n ≥ 5, y[n] = an−4(1 − a⁵)/(1 − a) → 0 because |a| < 1: the input has finite length and the stable system's response dies away.

Graphical view. Flip x[k] (or h[k]) and slide it. While 0 ≤ n ≤ 4 the flipped five-sample block only partly overlaps h[k], and the overlap grows by one sample each step; from n = 4 on it covers five samples of h, which shrink by the factor a each step.

Alternative route. The input is u[n] − u[n − 5], so by linearity and time invariance y[n] = s[n] − s[n − 5], where s[n] = (1 − an+1)/(1 − a) u[n] is the step response. For n ≥ 5 this gives (1 − an+1 − 1 + an−4)/(1 − a) = an−4(1 − a⁵)/(1 − a), the same as above.

Closing check. Σ y[n] should equal (Σ x)(Σ h) = 5 × 1/(1 − a). For a = 0.5: 10. The rising part gives 1 + 1.5 + 1.75 + 1.875 + 1.9375 = 8.0625 and the tail gives 0.96875/(1 − 0.5) = 1.9375; total 10.0.

bank.q: Solve y[n] − 0.5y[n − 1] = x[n] with zero initial condition for x[n] = u[n]; state whether the system is stable.
outline: Write the recursion y[n] = 0.5y[n − 1] + u[n] and iterate a few samples
Find the natural response from λ − 0.5 = 0
Find the forced response (a constant)
Fit the constant from y[0] and obtain y[n] = 2(1 − 0.5<sup>n+1</sup>)
Pole at 0.5 inside the unit circle: stable
answer: Recursive form. y[n] = 0.5y[n − 1] + x[n], with y[−1] = 0 and x[n] = 1 for n ≥ 0.
Natural response. With x = 0, try y = λⁿ: λⁿ − 0.5λn−1 = 0 gives λ − 0.5 = 0, so λ = 0.5 and ynat[n] = C(0.5)ⁿ.
Forced response. The input is a constant and λ = 1 is not a root, so try yforced = A: A − 0.5A = 1, so A = 2.
Total response. y[n] = 2 + C(0.5)ⁿ for n ≥ 0. From the recursion, y[0] = 1, so 2 + C = 1 and C = −1.
Answer. y[n] = [2 − (0.5)ⁿ]u[n], which can also be written 2(1 − 0.5n+1)u[n].
Second route. The impulse response is h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n] (iterate with x = δ: 1, 0.5, 0.25, …). Then y[n] = Σk=0n (0.5)k = (1 − 0.5n+1)/0.5, the same result.
Stability. The single pole (root) is λ = 0.5 and |0.5| < 1, so the causal system is BIBO stable. Equivalently Σ|h[n]| = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2 is finite.
Final value. As n → ∞, (0.5)ⁿ → 0 and y[n] → 2, which is the DC gain 1/(1 − 0.5) times the unit input.

Characteristic root versus pole. In Z-transform language H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹), with a pole at z = 0.5; the root λ = 0.5 of the characteristic equation is the same number, so both routes give the same stability verdict.

Transient and steady state. The output splits into the steady part 2 (the forced response) and the transient −(0.5)ⁿ (the natural response). The transient halves every sample: after 7 samples it is 0.0078, under 0.4% of the final value.
A non-zero start. If instead y[−1] = 2, then y[0] = 1 + 0.5 × 2 = 2, so C = 0 and y[n] = 2 for all n ≥ 0: the system starts already at its final value and shows no transient.
Closing check. n = 4: 2 − 0.0625 = 1.9375, the same as the iteration table.

bank.q: A uniform quantizer with n = 8 bits covers −5 V to +5 V. Find the step size, quantization noise power, and rms error.
outline: Noise power Δ²/12 ≈ 1.27 × 10⁻⁴ V²
rms error Δ/√12 ≈ 0.0113 V
State the uniform-error assumption and give the full-scale SQNR
answer: Levels. L = 2⁸ = 256 levels.
Step size. Δ = (xmax − xmin)/L = (5 − (−5))/256 = 10/256 = 0.0390625 V, about 39.1 mV.
Maximum error. Inside the range |eq| ≤ Δ/2 = 0.01953 V, about 19.5 mV.
Noise model. eq = Q(x) − x is taken as uniform on ±Δ/2 with zero mean, which holds for a busy signal that does not overload the quantizer.
rms error. erms = √Pq = Δ/√12 = 0.0390625/3.4641 = 0.011276 V, about 11.3 mV.
Formula check. 6.02 × 8 + 1.76 = 49.92 dB, agreeing with 49.93 dB (the 0.01 dB is rounding of 6.02).
Effect of one more bit. With 9 bits Δ halves to 0.0195 V, Pq falls by a factor of 4 and the SQNR rises by about 6 dB to 55.9 dB.
Overload. The model holds only while −5 V ≤ x ≤ +5 V. A 6 V peak is clipped to the top level, 5 − Δ/2 = 4.98 V, an error of about 1.02 V, far beyond Δ/2; such errors are not described by Δ²/12.
Smaller signals. A sine of amplitude 1 V (14 dB below full scale) gives SQNR = 49.92 − 20 log₁₀ 5 = 49.92 − 13.98 = 35.94 dB: the noise stays the same while the signal falls.

Mid-rise levels. The output levels are −5 + (k + ½)Δ for k = 0 to 255, from −4.98 V to +4.98 V; an input of 1.000 V lies in step k = 153 (from 0.977 V to 1.016 V), whose level is 0.996 V, an error of −0.004 V.
Closing check. Δ/√12 = 0.0113 V is smaller than the maximum error 0.0195 V, as an rms value of a uniform spread must be (ratio 1/√3 = 0.577).

bank.q: A band-pass signal occupies 20 kHz to 24 kHz. Derive a valid band-pass sampling rate below 2 × 24 kHz and check that aliases do not fall inside the band.
outline: f<sub>L</sub> = 20 kHz, f<sub>H</sub> = 24 kHz, B = 4 kHz
Use 2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1) with m ≤ ⌊f<sub>H</sub>/B⌋ = 6
List the ranges; m = 3 gives 16 kHz ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 20 kHz
Pick f<sub>s</sub> = 18 kHz
List the copies and check none overlaps 20 to 24 kHz
answer: Given. fL = 20 kHz, fH = 24 kHz, B = fH − fL = 4 kHz. Low-pass sampling would need fs > 2fH = 48 kHz.
Condition. The band must fit in one Nyquist zone, between (m − 1)fs/2 and mfs/2: mfs/2 ≥ fH and (m − 1)fs/2 ≤ fL, which gives 2fH/m ≤ fs ≤ 2fL/(m − 1) with 1 ≤ m ≤ ⌊fH/B⌋ = 6.
Choice. Take m = 3 and fs = 18 kHz, in the middle of 16 to 20 kHz so that there is margin on both sides. Zone 3 runs from 2 × 18/2 = 18 kHz to 3 × 18/2 = 27 kHz and contains 20 to 24 kHz.

answer.text: Copies. The band and its mirror image shifted by multiples of 18 kHz, on the positive axis up to 45 kHz:

answer: Image used. The copy at 2 to 6 kHz lies inside 0 to fs/2 = 9 kHz, the right way round because m = 3 is odd. A digital processor works on it directly; a band-pass filter from 20 to 24 kHz on the samples rebuilds the original.
Lowest rate. m = 6 gives exactly 8 kHz = 2B, but the copies then touch with no margin, so 8 kHz is the theoretical minimum, not a practical choice.

Why the zone test works. Sampling folds the axis at every multiple of fs/2. A band inside one zone is mapped one to one onto 0 to fs/2; a band that crosses a zone edge would be folded onto itself and overlap.
Margin at 18 kHz. The band edges sit 2 kHz above the zone's lower edge (20 − 18) and 3 kHz below its upper edge (27 − 24), so the anti-aliasing band-pass filter has 2 to 3 kHz of room on each side.
Closing check. 18 kHz < 48 kHz, the band 20 to 24 kHz sits inside zone 3 (18 to 27 kHz), and the nearest copies end at 16 kHz and start at 30 kHz.

bank.q: Compare ideal sinc reconstruction with zero-order hold reconstruction. Derive the aperture-effect sinc factor and discuss a compensation method.
outline: Ideal reconstruction: low-pass filter with cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 and gain T<sub>s</sub>, sinc kernel
Zero-order hold: rectangular pulse of width τ
Derive H(f) = τ sinc(fτ)e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>
Give the droop and phase numbers and what is left of the images
Compensate with an inverse-sinc equalizer, shorter pulses or oversampling
answer: Ideal reconstruction. The impulse samples pass through H(f) = Ts for |f| < fs/2, 0 elsewhere. In time this convolves the samples with h(t) = sinc(t/Ts), giving x(t) = Σ x(nTs) sinc((t − nTs)/Ts). It is exact for fs > 2fmax but needs a non-causal, infinitely long kernel and a vertical filter edge, so it cannot be built.

Zero-order hold. A DAC holds each sample constant for τ seconds (τ = Ts for a full hold), producing a staircase. Its impulse response is h0(t) = 1 for 0 ≤ t < τ and 0 elsewhere, so the staircase is xs(t) * h0(t).
Derivation. H0(f) = ∫ e−j2πft dt from 0 to τ = (1 − e−j2πfτ)/(j2πf).
Factor out e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>: H<sub>0</sub>(f) = e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>(e<sup>jπfτ</sup> − e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>)/(j2πf) = e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>·2j sin(πfτ)/(j2πf) = e<sup>−jπfτ</sup> sin(πfτ)/(πf).
Multiply and divide by τ: H0(f) = τ sinc(fτ) e−jπfτ. The magnitude τ|sinc(fτ)| is the aperture effect; the phase −πfτ is a pure delay of τ/2, which shapes nothing.
Output spectrum. The staircase spectrum is (1/Ts) Σ X(f − kfs) · τ sinc(fτ)e−jπfτ. The baseband copy is distorted by sinc(fτ), and the images are only partly removed.

answer.text: Numbers for fs = 8 kHz, τ = Ts = 125 μs.

answer: Comparison. The ideal filter is flat (0 dB) up to fs/2 and removes every image. The hold droops by 2.75 dB at the top of a 3.4 kHz speech band and leaves the image at 4.6 kHz only 5.38 dB down, so a smoothing analog low-pass filter must follow it.

Compensation 1: inverse-sinc equalizer. Before the DAC (digitally) or after it, apply gain 1/|sinc(fτ)| over the signal band: 1.026 at 1 kHz up to 1.373 at 3.4 kHz. Above the band the equalizer is not extended, because it would boost noise and images.
Compensation 2: shorter pulses. With τ = 10 μs the gain at 3.4 kHz is sinc(0.034) = 0.998 (−0.017 dB); the droop is negligible but the output pulses carry less energy.
Compensation 3: oversampling. At fs = 32 kHz with a full hold, fτ at 3.4 kHz is 3.4/32 = 0.106 and the gain is 0.982 (−0.16 dB), and the first image moves to 28.6 kHz, easy to filter.
Phase of the hold. The delay τ/2 = 62.5 μs adds a phase lag of πfτ radians: 0.425π = 76.5° at 3.4 kHz. Because it is linear in f it is a pure time delay and does not change the waveform shape.

Natural sampling compared. If the pulses followed the signal (natural sampling) instead of holding a value, the baseband copy would only be scaled by τ/Ts, with no droop; the aperture effect is a property of flat-top sampling and of the hold.
Where the equalizer goes. In a digital system the inverse-sinc response is easiest to build as a short FIR filter before the DAC; in an analog system it is a peaking stage in the smoothing filter.
Closing check. At fs/2 with τ = Ts the gain is sin(π/2)/(π/2) = 2/π = 0.637, the familiar −3.9 dB, and 1/0.637 = 1.571 is the largest equalizer gain any full-hold system needs.

bank.q: A sampled system shows a false 300 Hz tone when the input contains a 3.7 kHz component. Determine a possible sampling frequency, explain the alias, and specify the anti-aliasing filter.
outline: Solve |3700 − kf<sub>s</sub>| = 300 for possible rates; f<sub>s</sub> = 4 kHz is one
Explain folding about multiples of f<sub>s</sub>
Show the sample identity
Specify a filter before the sampler that removes 3.7 kHz
Find its order and check the attenuation at 3.7 kHz
answer: Condition. A tone at 3700 Hz is seen at 300 Hz when |3700 − kfs| = 300 for some integer k, that is kfs = 4000 Hz or kfs = 3400 Hz.
Most likely. fs = 4 kHz, a common rate; its Nyquist frequency is 2 kHz and 3.7 kHz is far above it.

Folding. The copy of the spectrum centred at fs = 4 kHz carries the 3.7 kHz line to 4000 − 3700 = 300 Hz inside the baseband 0 to 2 kHz. In samples: cos(2π·3700n/4000) = cos(2πn − 2π·300n/4000) = cos(2π·300n/4000) for every integer n.
Not removable afterwards. The false tone is now made of the same numbers as a real 300 Hz tone; a digital filter would remove the wanted 300 Hz content too.

Filter edges. Suppose the wanted signal reaches fmax = 1.5 kHz. Passband edge fc = 1.5 kHz; anything above fs − fmax = 2.5 kHz would fold into 0 to 1.5 kHz, so the stopband edge is 2.5 kHz. Ask for A = 40 dB there.
Order. N ≥ log₁₀(104 − 1)/(2 log₁₀(2.5/1.5)) = 4.000/(2 × 0.2218) = 9.02, so N = 10 (a 9th-order filter would just miss 40 dB).
At 3.7 kHz. Attenuation = 10 log₁₀(1 + (3.7/1.5)20) = 10 log₁₀(1 + 2.466720) = 78.4 dB. A 1 V interferer now reaches the sampler at about 0.12 mV, and its 300 Hz alias is buried in the noise.
Alternative. Raise fs. At fs = 8 kHz, 3.7 kHz is below fs/2 = 4 kHz and is not aliased at all; a digital filter can then remove it.

Why 4 kHz is the likely answer. Of the candidates, only rates above 2 × 300 = 600 Hz can show a 300 Hz tone at all, and a system meant to carry signals up to about 1.5–2 kHz would use a rate near 4 kHz; the lower rates would alias much of the wanted band too.
Check of another candidate. At fs = 3.4 kHz: |3700 − 3400| = 300 Hz as well. Either rate is a valid answer if it is stated with this check.
Closing check. With fs = 4 kHz, |3700 − 4000| = 300 Hz, the observed tone; the filter must act before the sampler, with cutoff below fs/2 = 2 kHz.

bank.q: For a second-order difference equation with poles at z = 0.8 and z = −0.6, discuss stability and natural response. What changes if a pole moves to z = 1.2?
outline: Build the characteristic equation and the difference equation
Both roots inside the unit circle: stable
Natural response C<sub>1</sub>(0.8)ⁿ + C<sub>2</sub>(−0.6)ⁿ, both decaying; find h[n] as an example
With a root at 1.2 the mode 1.2ⁿ grows: unstable
Compare h[10] in the two cases
answer: Characteristic equation. Roots 0.8 and −0.6 give (λ − 0.8)(λ + 0.6) = λ² − 0.2λ − 0.48 = 0, so the system (with only b0 = 1) is y[n] − 0.2y[n − 1] − 0.48y[n − 2] = x[n].
Stability. |0.8| < 1 and |−0.6| = 0.6 < 1: both roots are inside the unit circle, so the causal system is BIBO stable.

Natural response. ynat[n] = C1(0.8)ⁿ + C2(−0.6)ⁿ. The first term decays smoothly; the second alternates in sign and decays faster. After 10 samples (0.8)10 = 0.107 and (0.6)10 = 0.006, so the 0.8 mode dominates.
Impulse response. h[0] = 1 and h[1] = 0.2 from the recursion. C1 + C2 = 1 and 0.8C1 − 0.6C2 = 0.2 give 1.4C1 = 0.8, so C1 = 4/7 and C2 = 3/7: h[n] = [(4/7)(0.8)ⁿ + (3/7)(−0.6)ⁿ]u[n].
Pole moved to 1.2. Now (λ − 1.2)(λ + 0.6) = λ² − 0.6λ − 0.72, so y[n] − 0.6y[n − 1] − 0.72y[n − 2] = x[n]. The root 1.2 is outside the unit circle.
New impulse response. h[0] = 1, h[1] = 0.6. C1 + C2 = 1 and 1.2C1 − 0.6C2 = 0.6 give 1.8C1 = 1.2, so C1 = 2/3 and C2 = 1/3: h[n] = (2/3)(1.2)ⁿ + (1/3)(−0.6)ⁿ.

Growth. h[10] = (2/3)(6.192) + (1/3)(0.006) = 4.130 (iteration gives 4.1298), and h[n] keeps growing by about 20% per sample. Σ|h[n]| diverges, so the system is unstable: even a single impulse gives an unbounded output.

Evaluation. Stability depends only on the root magnitudes. Moving one root from 0.8 to 1.2 changes a response that dies to 6% of its start by n = 10 into one four times its start and growing. In a real filter such a move can come from rounding coefficients, so designers keep poles well inside the circle.

Marginal case. If the root moved to exactly z = 1, the mode would be a constant C1: the impulse response would not decay, Σ|h[n]| would diverge, and a step input would make the output grow like n. So the boundary itself is already not BIBO stable.
Negative root behaviour. The (−0.6)ⁿ term flips sign every sample, so h[n] ripples: h[2] = 0.52 is larger than h[1] = 0.2. This ripple comes from the negative pole, not from instability.

bank.q: Analyse an end-to-end chain: analog anti-aliasing filter, sampler, n-bit quantizer, discrete-time LTI filter, and reconstruction filter. Explain how each block affects aliasing, quantization noise, and stability, and give design trade-offs.
outline: Anti-aliasing filter limits the input band before sampling
Sampler must satisfy f<sub>s</sub> > 2f<sub>max</sub> or aliasing appears
n-bit quantizer adds noise of power Δ²/12; SQNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB
The discrete-time filter shapes signal and noise and must be stable
The hold and reconstruction filter remove images and droop by sinc(fτ)
Trade-offs: filter order, sampling rate, word length and cost
answer: The chain. x(t) → analog anti-aliasing filter → sampler at fs → n-bit quantizer → discrete-time LTI filter → DAC with zero-order hold → analog reconstruction filter → output. Take speech up to fmax = 3.4 kHz as the running example.

1. Anti-aliasing filter (aliasing). It removes everything that would fold into 0 to 3.4 kHz, that is above fs − fmax. For 30 dB at that edge with a Butterworth filter (fc = 3.4 kHz): at fs = 8 kHz the edge is 4.6 kHz and N = 12; at fs = 16 kHz the edge is 12.6 kHz and N = 3.

2. Sampler (aliasing). fs must exceed 2fmax = 6.8 kHz. At 8 kHz the guard band is 1.2 kHz; at 16 kHz it is 9.2 kHz. Without the filter, a 4.7 kHz noise component at fs = 8 kHz would appear at 3.3 kHz, inside the speech band.

3. Quantizer (noise). For an n-bit uniform quantizer over ±1 V, Δ = 2/2ⁿ and Pq = Δ²/12. With n = 8: Δ = 7.81 mV and SQNR = 6.02 × 8 + 1.76 = 49.9 dB for a full-scale sine; with n = 12: 74.0 dB. Overload must be avoided, so the input level is set a few dB below full scale, which costs the same number of dB of SQNR.

4. Discrete-time filter (shaping and stability). Take y[n] = 0.5y[n − 1] + 0.5x[n]: pole at 0.5, inside the unit circle, so stable, with DC gain 0.5/(1 − 0.5) = 1. Its h[n] = 0.5(0.5)ⁿu[n] gives a noise power gain Σh² = 0.25/(1 − 0.25) = 1/3, so white quantization noise is cut by 4.8 dB. A pole outside the unit circle would make the output grow without bound whatever the input.
So this simple low-pass also cuts the top of the speech band by 9.3 dB: the trade-off between noise reduction and bandwidth is set by the pole position.

5. Zero-order hold and reconstruction filter (images and droop). With τ = Ts = 125 μs the hold has gain sinc(0.425) = 0.728 (−2.75 dB) at 3.4 kHz, corrected by an inverse-sinc gain of 1.37. The image of 3.4 kHz at 4.6 kHz is only 5.4 dB down after the hold, so an analog smoothing filter with the same edges as the anti-aliasing filter must follow.

6. Trade-offs. Higher fs: simpler analog filters (order 12 → 3), smaller droop, but more samples, more power and more memory. More bits: 6 dB of SQNR per bit, but a costlier converter. Sharper discrete-time filters: better noise rejection, but more multipliers and poles closer to the unit circle, which are sensitive to coefficient rounding.

head: Block
Choice
Number
rows: N = 12 at 8 kHz, N = 3 at 16 kHz
stable, noise −4.8 dB, −9.3 dB at 3.4 kHz

answer: Where noise enters and leaves. Quantization noise is added after the sampler, so the anti-aliasing filter does not reduce it; the discrete-time filter and the reconstruction filter do, by removing noise outside the signal band. Oversampling spreads the same Δ²/12 over a wider band, so a digital filter can remove more of it: doubling fs lowers the in-band noise by about 3 dB.

Stability across the chain. The analog filters and the hold are stable by construction (passive or with poles in the left half-plane). The only block that can become unstable is a recursive discrete-time filter, and only when a pole lies on or outside the unit circle; rounding its coefficients to the word length can move a pole near the circle, so poles are kept well inside it.

Aliasing in the output side. The output side has the mirror problem: the images at kfs ± f must be removed by the reconstruction filter, or they are heard as high-pitched tones. The same guard band that eases the anti-aliasing filter eases the reconstruction filter.
Closing check. 8 kHz > 6.8 kHz (no aliasing of the wanted band), the only pole 0.5 is inside the unit circle (stable), and 49.9 dB = 6.02 × 8 + 1.76 dB.

glossary.def: Taking the values of a continuous-time signal at the instants nT<sub>s</sub>.
A signal whose Fourier transform is zero above some highest frequency f<sub>max</sub>.
The minimum sampling rate 2f<sub>max</sub> for a signal band-limited to f<sub>max</sub>.
Half the sampling rate, f<sub>s</sub>/2; components below it are kept, components above it fold.
The longest allowed sample spacing, 1/(2f<sub>max</sub>).
Recovering the continuous-time signal from its samples, ideally with a low-pass filter of cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2 and gain T<sub>s</sub>.
sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu), with sinc(0) = 1; the ideal interpolation kernel.
The empty gap from f<sub>max</sub> to f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>max</sub> between the baseband and the first spectral copy; its width is f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>max</sub>.
A false lower frequency produced when spectral copies overlap.
An analog low-pass filter before the sampler that removes components that would fold into the wanted band.
Sampling a band from f<sub>L</sub> to f<sub>H</sub> at a rate below 2f<sub>H</sub>, allowed when 2f<sub>H</sub>/m ≤ f<sub>s</sub> ≤ 2f<sub>L</sub>/(m − 1).
A strip of width f<sub>s</sub>/2, from (m − 1)f<sub>s</sub>/2 to mf<sub>s</sub>/2; a band inside one zone can be sampled without overlap.
Sampling with narrow pulses whose tops follow the signal; each spectral copy keeps its shape.
Sampling in which each value is held constant for τ seconds, as in a sample-and-hold circuit.
The high-frequency droop sinc(fτ) caused by flat-top sampling or a zero-order hold.
Holding each sample constant until the next one; its response is τ sinc(fτ)e<sup>−jπfτ</sup>.
Mapping each sample amplitude to the nearest of a finite set of levels.
The spacing Δ between adjacent levels of a uniform quantizer, also called its resolution.
e<sub>q</sub> = Q(x) − x, the quantized value minus the true sample; within ±Δ/2 without overload.
Signal-to-quantization-noise ratio; 6.02n + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine and n bits.
Compressing large amplitudes before uniform quantization and expanding them after (μ-law, A-law).
δ[n] = 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere; the identity element of convolution.
The output h[n] of an LTI system to δ[n], with the system at rest.
y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k], the output of a discrete-time LTI system.
An equation relating the present output to past outputs and to present and past inputs with constant coefficients.
The roots of λ<sup>N</sup> + a<sub>1</sub>λ<sup>N−1</sup> + … + a<sub>N</sub> = 0; the natural modes, or poles, of the system.
Every bounded input gives a bounded output; for an LTI system Σ|h[n]| is finite, for a causal LCCDE every |λ<sub>i</sub>| < 1.
Finite and infinite impulse response: non-recursive and recursive difference equations.
